title: An AI-native org isn't everyone using AI — it's assuming the org doesn't exist and rewriting it
dek: Lockin merged HR and IT into HARO, put a technical founder type in charge of people and AI; circle leads get the bonus pool and the right to allocate it, and hiring requires proving AI can't do the job.
why: The founder of a 12-year hardware company explains the concrete mechanics of rewriting an organization: HARO, circles, AI management trainees, how FDEs actually land — with details and the pitfalls.
who: Founders, HR leaders and business owners pushing an AI org transformation, especially at hardware or consumer electronics companies who want to move the org but don't know where to start.
skip: After 1:04:25 the chit-chat and outro music can be skipped.

points.h: AI-native starts by assuming the organization doesn't exist
points.body: Chen Bin's definition of an AI-native organization is not ‘everyone should use AI well’ but starting from AI and asking again: can AI do this thing, and as far as possible don't let a person do it. The harsher step is to assume the original organization and processes don't exist — ‘they shouldn't even exist’ — and go back to the state of a single founder starting a company to redesign roles and processes. So this is not accelerating existing processes, it's tearing the processes down first and rebuilding. He admits this is mainly aimed at the core org builders, not a slogan shouted at everyone.

points.h: HARO's head comes from technology, not HR
points.body: Lockin merged HR and IT into HARO (Human AI Resource Office), but Chen Bin stresses it is not an ordinary HR+IT: the head must understand the business, and the person chosen is an old partner who started the company with him and has done technology, product, CEO, R&D, brand and IT. The logic is inverted — the old HR head leaned toward people and was insensitive to AI, so now a technology-oriented person runs it, with HR BPs who are sensitive to people assigned to him. Under this department sit the AIO (the former IT team, which will do Agent Builder work) on a solid line, and FDEs reporting on a dotted line.

points.h: Agent Builder and FDE are two kinds of people in the short term
points.body: Chen Bin draws the line clearly: an Agent Builder leans technical and can build an Agent; an FDE has to go into the business front line, map out supply, planning and procurement processes, and is best a business expert. Long term one person might cover both; short term it must be two kinds of people working together. They did not copy Anker's approach of pulling people out of work and locking them away for a month, because they don't have that much slack; instead people from the business spend 30% to 50% of their energy doing AI-ification alongside their day jobs. The company also set up AI proficiency levels L1 to L4, with L2 and above called ‘AI 起航员’ (AI navigators) and above that ‘领航员’ (pilots).

points.h: Circles erase functional power; the circle lead gets the bonus pool
points.body: Lockin's circles differ from project teams and from Huawei's matrix: a matrix is a dual line of product line and function, while a circle is a small team around an end-to-end value loop, deliberately erasing functional power and boundaries so the circle lead's power grows. The company gives the circle a bonus pool, and the circle lead decides how to split it — even how much to give himself — while HR and functional departments only have an advisory voice. Chen Bin says at this stage the ‘fighting’ line dominates; the functional line may in future become something like a technology committee, but within the first half year to a year of the change, the front line gets to decide.

points.h: Experience can become a burden instead
points.body: Chen Bin says AI management trainees naturally started using AI from university in 2023, have no fear about doing things, and use it more than the veterans. His exact words: ‘sometimes experience instead becomes a burden’, and the worst is the half-informed — whose experience hasn't arrived but who feel they are very experienced and can't change. Veterans have framework thinking and systematic thinking as their foundation, but on which processes and which roles can be removed, the clear-eyed judge more easily. The bar for AI management trainees is internal AI level L2 or above, requiring skill with skills and building Agents; only L3 can author workflows.

points.h: R&D turns fast, marketing turns slow
points.body: Chen Bin admits the speed of transformation varies a lot by department: technical R&D tied to software and coding is easiest, since writing code every day gives immediate positive feedback; marketing and branding are slow, because after publishing more content they ask ‘so what’ — did it bring revenue growth and a bigger bonus. He also mentions a real conflict: people doing design and content feel AI can only accelerate quantity, not raise quality, and 60-point output doesn't stick around. His response is to give everyone an operating mindset: whether content brings conversion is the standard.

points.h: Three rounds of sign-ups: stand up again, then sit down again
points.body: Lockin ran three internal rounds of sign-ups: the first for incremental roles, such as the company-level ten or twenty Agents and the corresponding Agent Builders and FDEs; the second for roles missing after circles formed, such as a content marketing Agent Builder; the third to keep filling gaps. Applicants first do a self-assessment to find what they're good at, then give a three-to-five-minute defense, and after the judges score, AI is used to analyze the meeting minutes and the talks for matching. Of a hundred applicants, twenty or thirty may finally be chosen. Chen Bin says both the mechanism and the results are very good.

points.h: To hire, you must first prove AI can't do the job
points.body: After people from the original departments are picked off by circles, when a boss wants to add headcount there are logically only two channels: find an AI management trainee, or use more AI tokens. If you really must hire again, it goes to Chen Bin for special approval, and you have to explain clearly why a management trainee won't do and why AI won't do. Chen Bin says ‘logically he has no channel left’. They plan to hire 50 AI management trainees by year-end, and are already close to 20. Xiaofei's role at Lockin is like a strategic HR, a CHO as a service, working with Chen Bin on the AI-native transformation.

points.h: IPD is not overturned, only accelerated
points.body: Chen Bin says inside the company he is in fact the most radical one, and people often pull him back and ask for more caution. On sedimented systems like Huawei's IPD, his judgment is: AI can only remake processes that were already unreasonable and especially redundant; IPD itself is very reasonable and can only be accelerated. For example, from strategy to execution, SP to BP, used to take three months to half a year, now two months, doubling efficiency, but the nodes like 五看三定 (five looks, three settings) are still there, just three weeks become three days. Training a product line manager used to take 10 to 15 years, now three to five, but the rotations that must happen cannot be skipped.

points.h: Not every company should run this fast
points.body: Chen Bin's advice to three kinds of bosses — milk tea shops, PCB factories, call centers — is to look at the real value AI brings in that industry: the more traditional the industry, the lower the value, and you can wait until platforms like Doubao and Volcano Engine mature before choosing, with lower trial-and-error cost. But the more frontier the tech company, the earlier it should embrace AI, because technology changes a lot and the market changes fast, and decision quality matters more. He specifically notes that before physical AI takes off, PCB factories and the like should be cautious and not move first; milk tea shops are driven more by channels and operations, and AI can quickly build a feedback loop from the user side to the supply chain side, so its effect is greater.

quotes.text: I think an AI-native organization probably starts from AI first — whatever AI can do, don't have a person do it. Think with that AI-native mindset first, and even the process, logically, should be restructured.

It used to be functional, right? Now I'm an end-to-end small team around a value loop, and I even deliberately erase the functional power, or the boundaries — make functional power smaller, make the circle's power, or the circle lead's power, bigger.

Sometimes experience instead becomes a burden. It's better to have it — but the half-informed are the scary ones: their experience hasn't arrived yet, but they feel they're already very experienced, right? They can't change.

As far as possible we fill with AI, right? Prioritize AI — whatever AI can fill, let AI fill it. Unless it can't be filled. And if it can't be filled, internally we say: either you say you'll find an AI management trainee to fill it, or you use more AI tokens.

It used to take at least three months to half a year; now we do SP to BP in two months, right? At least double the efficiency. But the process itself hasn't changed — it's just that where I used to hold five meetings, now it's three meetings, two meetings.

Look at the real value AI brings in that industry. I think the more traditional the industry, the lower the value it brings, indeed a bit lower. And if it's lower, then you can reasonably say you can wait until these — people like us who jump into the pit and play around, right? — or until things like Doubao, Volcano Engine, the ones doing better, and then you choose. That's fine.
